title: From a news feed to a backtest

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A headline says a company is doing great. Another says it's in trouble. How do you know which one actually moved the stock, or whether either mattered?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That's a tough one. Is that what AINewsTracker is for?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sort of. Antoine's write-up is about a FastAPI service that turns financial news into records you can search, analyse and compare with market data. It's not a magic predictor. It's plumbing that keeps things traceable.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay, so how does a story travel through it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A request starts a collection job. The news service pulls feed content and creates article records. A metrics service analyses the text, and the result is stored in MongoDB. Routes take the HTTP requests, services do the work, repositories hide the database. Redis handles caching.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Neat separation. What does the analysis actually produce?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: According to the documentation, a sentiment label and score, detected tickers, a summary and topic labels. And here's the part Antoine cares about: each article keeps its source, its URL, its publication date and its text next to those fields.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So you can trace a sentiment label back to the publisher.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. And the ticker lets you connect mentions across articles without treating every spelling of a company name as a different business.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Then there's the backtesting side. The strategy route sends requests to a trading module, so you can test strategies on history.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: But he's careful there, isn't he?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Very. He says he'd read the original text beside the outputs before using them. A summary can drop a condition, and a company mention doesn't mean there's a tradable event. Labels are inputs to an experiment. They don't prove a news item caused a market move, and a backtest doesn't guarantee future performance.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He even gives a checklist: collection, text analysis, strategy input, backtest output. For each one, what to inspect. Like whether the data was actually available at the moment being tested.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the article says plainly that it presents no measured accuracy or trading returns.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good honesty. So the takeaway is keep the source attached to the analysis.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Right. The full write-up has the architecture diagram, with every node linking to its source file.
